title: A hymn in Jaijavanti
hookLine: it's passing, it's passing: Guru Tegh Bahadur talks to the mind about time, and the week looks back

cards: Departing. Departing. On a station board the word blinks beside a train that hasn't moved yet.
The doors are still open. People are walking, not running. The word isn't a disaster; it's information, said twice so nobody misses it.
Guru Tegh Bahadur has a hymn in Jaijavanti that opens the same way, with one word said twice: it's passing, it's passing. It's the last day of this week, so there's a look back over the ragas, too.
But first, the board, and the doors still open.

teach.h: O MIND, WHAT WILL BECOME OF YOU?
teach.b: The hymns in Jaijavanti keep speaking to the mind directly. One asks it: O mind, what will become of you?

This one opens, in paraphrase: it is passing, it is passing, your life is passing to no purpose. Day and night you hear holy stories, and still you don't take them in, the same charge Parmanand made in Sarang.
The time has come; where will you run? The body you counted on as steady will turn to dust. Why not remember the Name of the Lord?
In Gurmukhi the opening is beet jaihai, beet jaihai, and the doubling does what the station board does. It isn't shouting. It's making sure.
The hymn is blunt, even calling the mind a fool, but it isn't despair. It names time honestly, and in the same breath points to what can still be done: remember.

teach.h: NOT A THREAT: THE DOORS ARE OPEN.
teach.b: The doors are open. Yesterday's hymn said remembering is your work; today's says the work has a clock.

teach.h: THE WEEK: STRANGER, CHILD, LIGHT, SAND.
teach.b: Now the week. Guru Arjan in Kanara: no enemy, no stranger. Kalyan in the evening: we are your children, and the bee that comes back again and again.
Prabhati at dawn: the Name as the ornament you put on first, and Kabir's one light on every street. Jaijavanti, where the ragas end: remember, this is your work. And today, the reason to start now.
Evening, dawn and the end of the ragas, with the same Name running through all of them.

how: Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns, including those in Jaijavanti, are sung in kirtan; his saloks near the end of the Granth are also read at the close of a full reading.

o: remember the Name of the Lord.
games.why: the hymn asks why not remember the Name; the doors are still open.

practice: If you can, play Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn of beet jaihai, or another in Jaijavanti; if not, sit in the quiet and feel this breath come in and go out, passing, and the next one passing too.
Don't hold on, and don't hurry: be present for each one before it goes, the way you'd step through open doors without running.
If you pray, remember the Name on each breath, as the hymn asks; if you don't, let each breath be fully noticed before it slips by.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Jaijavanti. Guru Tegh Bahadur's song to the mind: it's passing, it's passing; why not remember the Name while there's time? Today's word.
